unit.title: Perform machining operations using horizontal and/or vertical boring machines

summary: This unit teaches you to bore holes accurately on horizontal boring machines and vertical boring mills. You will learn how the machines work, how to work safely on them, how to lift, clamp and set up heavy work, how to choose boring tools, speeds and feeds, and how to drill, bore, line bore and face to size. You will also learn to measure bores, find and cure common faults, and finish the job and care for the machine.

blocks.p: **Boring** means enlarging an existing hole with a single-point cutting tool, to an exact **size**, in an exact **position**, with a good **finish**. A drill makes a hole quickly, but drilled holes wander, are not perfectly round and are seldom exactly to size. A boring tool follows the machine's spindle, so it can correct all three.

Boring machines handle work that is too big or too heavy for an ordinary lathe or milling machine: pump and gearbox casings, machine frames, large flanges and wheels, and fabricated parts such as brackets, hinges and the pin bosses of excavator buckets. Welders meet boring because holes in welded parts are often **bored after welding**: the heat of welding pulls the part out of shape, so holes made before welding would end up out of line.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other training centres. Your Centre may not have a boring machine. If it does not, you will do the same work on a vertical milling machine with a boring head, and the methods in this kit still apply.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the machine shop
rows: Follow the machine's safety rules: guards, dress, no gloves near turning parts, isolation, chip and fluid handling, safe lifting.
Name the main parts of horizontal and vertical boring machines, what moves on each, and the work each suits best.
Read each hole's size, tolerance, position and finish, and the datum faces; plan the order of operations.
Lift, hold and set up the work
Lift with rated gear; clamp securely on parallels and packing; set the work square; find the datum or the centre of a hole.
Pick a rigid boring bar or head and a suitable tool tip; work out the spindle speed; set the feed and depth of cut.
Centre drill, drill, rough bore, measure, adjust and finish bore; line bore and face where the drawing asks.
Measure bores with the right instruments, compare them with the tolerance, and record the sizes.
Recognise chatter, taper, bellmouth, ovality and poor finish, and know their causes and cures.
Finish and care for the machine
Deburr, clean, lubricate, store tools, and report faults.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the machines, tools, set-up, work holding, speeds and feeds, boring operations, measuring, faults, safety and machine care.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as insert, reamer, T-slot, step block, parallels, tolerance, ovality, eyebolt, headstock, and speed sums) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** in a group: drilling and boring a 32 mm hole to a tolerance of +0.05/−0.00 mm in a block, and line boring the two lugs of a fabricated bracket so that a test bar slides through both. The assessor checks every set-up before the spindle is started.

blocks.note: Bring a calculator. You must be able to work out a spindle speed from N = (Vc × 1000) ÷ (π × D) quickly and correctly, and to work out how far to move a boring tool.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Boring machines and what they do

blocks.p: On a **horizontal boring machine** the spindle points **sideways**, across the table. It is like a very large, very rigid drilling and milling machine laid on its side. The work stays still on the table while the tool turns.

head: Part
What it does
rows: The heavy base. It carries the table and the column on accurate slideways.
The upright that carries the headstock.
Moves **up and down the column**. It holds the motor drive, the gearbox and the spindle.
Turns the tool. It can also slide out of the headstock (be fed in and out) to bore deep holes.
Carries the work. It moves along and across the bed on its saddle, and on many machines it can rotate, so several faces can be machined in one set-up.
A second column at the far end of the table, with a bearing that holds the outer end of a long boring bar for line boring.
On some machines: a slide on the spindle nose that carries a tool outwards across a face, to face large flat surfaces.
Handwheels with graduated dials, power feeds and, on many machines, a digital readout (DRO) showing the position of each slide.

blocks.p: **Best for:** large, heavy, box-shaped parts with holes in their sides: gearbox and pump casings, machine frames, engine blocks, bearing housings, and fabricated brackets with holes in two or more walls that must be **in line**.

A **vertical boring mill** is like a large lathe standing on end. Its other common name is the **vertical turret lathe (VTL)**. Here the **work turns** on a large round table, and the tools are fed into it.

head: Part
What it does
rows: The table is a large turning faceplate, with jaws or clamps to hold the work. It is the part that rotates.
One or two uprights beside the table.
A horizontal beam that moves up and down the columns.
Slide across the rail and feed their tools down (vertically) or across (horizontally). One may carry a turret holding several tools.
On some machines: a tool head on the column that feeds into the side of the work.

blocks.p: **Best for:** large, heavy, round parts: flanges, rings, wheels, pulleys, large gear blanks and valve bodies. The work is faced, turned on the outside and bored on the inside.

head: Point
Horizontal boring machine
Vertical boring mill (VTL)
rows: Tools fed vertically and across; the table's axis is vertical
What moves to position the cut
Table (along and across), headstock (up and down), spindle (in and out)
Cross rail (up and down), rail heads (across and down)
Box-shaped parts; holes in side walls; in-line holes
Round parts; faces, outside diameters and bores
Drilling, boring, line boring, facing, counterboring, spot facing, tapping, milling
Facing, turning, boring, grooving, taper turning

blocks.note: If your Centre has no boring machine, a **vertical milling machine with an adjustable boring head** does the same kind of work on smaller parts: the spindle turns the boring tool, the work is clamped on the table, and the table positions the hole.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Boring machines are big, slow and powerful. They will not stall if they catch your sleeve, your glove or your hair: they will pull you in. Heavy work and heavy fittings can crush hands and feet. Follow these rules every time.

ul: Use a machine only after you have been trained on it and given permission.
Wear **safety glasses**, **safety boots** and close-fitting overalls. Button or roll up sleeves, take off rings, watches and chains, and tie back long hair.
**No gloves near the turning spindle, boring bar or table.** A glove can be caught and drag your hand in. Wear gloves only to handle sharp work or chips with the machine stopped.
Check the guards, the emergency stop and the area around the machine. Keep the floor clear and dry.
Keep the table's travel clear, so the work cannot hit the column, a support or a person when the table moves.
Remove all spanners, keys and loose tools from the machine before starting.
At the Centre, the **assessor or instructor checks the set-up** before the spindle is started.
Stay at the machine. Never leave it running unattended.

Never reach across or over a turning table, spindle or bar. On a vertical boring mill, the table's jaws and the work can stick out beyond its edge: keep the barrier or guard rail in place and stand clear.
**Stop the spindle (or table) fully** before you measure, adjust the tool, clear chips or touch the work.
Clear chips with a **brush or chip hook**, never with your hands, and never with compressed air blown towards anyone. Chips are razor sharp and often hot.
Keep your face out of the line of flying chips; use the chip guard.

Stop the spindle **and isolate the machine** (switch off at the isolator, and lock it off where the Centre uses locks and tags) before changing a boring bar, head, tool tip or nozzle, or reaching into the machine. The stop button alone is not enough: someone could press start.
Handle tool tips and boring heads with care: carbide tips are sharp and chip easily if dropped.

Lift heavy castings and fabrications with a **crane or hoist** and **rated slings** or **eyebolts**, never by hand. Check that each sling or eyebolt is marked with its **safe working load (SWL)** and that the load is within it.
An **eyebolt** must be screwed fully into a sound tapped hole, with its collar seated flat on the work, and the pull must be in line with it. A sideways pull on an eyebolt can bend or break it.
Only a trained person operates the crane or gives the signals. Never stand or put your hands under a raised load; keep fingers out of pinch points as the work is lowered.
Lower the work onto parallels or packing, not straight onto the table, so slings can be removed and the table is not damaged.
**Cast iron** is usually cut dry and makes fine black dust: wear a dust mask and use extraction where it is fitted.
Cutting fluid can irritate the skin and cause dermatitis. Keep skin contact low, use barrier cream if the Centre provides it, wash your hands before eating, and report any rash.
Wipe up spills at once so nobody slips. Never put oily rags in your pockets.

blocks.note: Isolation means cutting the machine off from its power so it cannot start. Where the Centre uses lock-off, fit your own lock and tag to the isolator, try the start button to prove it will not start, and remove your lock only when you have finished and the guards are back.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Planning and setting up the work

blocks.p: For each hole, find on the drawing:

ul: **Size:** the diameter and depth.
**Tolerance:** how much the size may vary, for example 40.00 +0.03/−0.00 mm.
**Position:** its distance from the datum faces or edges, and from other holes.
**Finish:** how smooth the wall must be.
**Datum faces:** the faces all positions are measured from, and the faces that must be square to the bore.

blocks.p: Then plan the order of operations and the tools for each one, and write them on the job sheet with the speeds you have worked out.

head: Item
What it is and does
rows: The slotted grooves along the machine table that hold the heads of clamping bolts
Bolts whose heads slide in the T-slots, used with clamps
A flat bar with a bolt through a slot in the middle: one end presses on the work, the other on a packing block. Also called a bar, heel or toe clamp.
A stepped steel block that supports the end of a clamp at the right height
Steel or hardwood blocks used to support the clamp end or the work
A matched pair of accurate, hardened steel bars that raise the work evenly off the table, so the tool can pass right through without cutting the table
An accurate L-shaped plate for holding work at 90° to the table
Small adjustable supports placed under overhanging parts of the work so they do not spring under the clamp or the cut

ul: Clean the table and the underside of the work first, and file off burrs. A chip or burr under the work tilts it.
Clamp **close to where the cut will be**, and **over solid support**, so the work cannot spring or vibrate.
Put the clamp bolt **as close to the work as possible**. The clamping force is shared between the work and the packing: the nearer the bolt is to the work, the more of the force goes onto the work.

Set the packing **level with, or just above**, the clamping face of the work, so the clamp presses down squarely. If the packing is too low, the clamp tilts and grips only with its edge, and the work can move.
Never clamp across a thin, unsupported wall or across the hole to be bored: the work will distort, and the bore will be out of round when the clamp is released.
Put soft packing (copper, aluminium or card) under clamps on finished faces, to avoid marking them.
Tighten the clamps evenly and firmly. On thin castings, tighten just enough to hold, and check with a dial indicator that the work has not been pulled out of shape.

flow: Fix a dial indicator to the spindle or headstock, with its plunger touching the datum face of the work
Move the table so the indicator runs along the face, and watch the reading
If the reading changes, tap the work round with a soft hammer until the reading stays the same along the face
Tighten the clamps, then run the indicator along the face again to check that nothing moved

blocks.h: Finding the datum or a hole centre

head: Method
How it works
rows: Held in the spindle and run at the slow speed its maker gives. Move the work towards it until the tip kicks sideways: the spindle centre is then half the tip's diameter from the edge (for example 5 mm for a 10 mm tip). Set the dial or readout to that figure.

To centre the spindle on an existing hole: fit a dial indicator to the spindle so its plunger touches the bore wall, turn the spindle slowly by hand, and move the table until the reading is the same all the way round.
Once the datum is set, move to each hole position using the graduated dials or the digital readout.

blocks.note: Handwheel screws have a little play, called **backlash**. Always move to a position from the same direction, and if you overshoot, wind back past it and come up to it again. Lock any slide that must not move during the cut.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **boring bar** is a bar that holds a cutting tool and cuts the inside of a hole as it turns. The bar must be **stiff**, because the cutting force bends it, and a bending bar gives chatter, taper and wrong sizes.

head: Type
Use
rows: Short (stub) boring bar, held at one end
Most single holes. Rigidity depends on the bar's diameter and how far it sticks out (its overhang).
Line-boring bar, supported at both ends
A long bar passed through two or more walls, held in the spindle at one end and in the end support at the other; used for line boring.
Fits in the spindle and holds a small boring bar on a slide. A fine screw with a graduated dial moves the tool out from the centre in small, exact steps to change the bore size.
Feeds a tool outwards across a face while the spindle turns, to face large surfaces square to the bore.

ul: Use the **thickest bar** that fits the hole with room for the chips.
Use the **shortest overhang** that reaches the bottom of the cut.

As a guide, a solid steel boring bar should not stick out more than about **4 times its own diameter** (100 mm for a 25 mm bar). Bars of carbide or special damped bars can reach further: follow the maker's figures.
Support long bars at both ends whenever you can.

head: Material
Points to know
rows: Tough; can be ground to shape on a tool grinder
Good for small bores and interrupted cuts
Much harder; keeps a sharp edge at much higher cutting speeds and temperatures
More brittle: chips if knocked or if the bar chatters
Brazed tips are ground with special wheels, not on an ordinary bench grinder
Small carbide tips clamped in a holder
When one corner wears, the insert is turned (indexed) to a fresh edge, then replaced when all edges are worn
The shape, grade and nose radius are chosen from the maker's chart

blocks.p: A larger **nose radius** on the tip gives a smoother finish, but it pushes harder on the bar and can make a long bar chatter. A small radius is kinder to a slender bar.

blocks.h: Other tools used on boring machines

head: Tool
Use
rows: Short and stiff; starts a hole in the right place without wandering
Make the hole and open it up, leaving metal for boring
A fluted tool that finishes a drilled or bored hole to an exact size with a smooth wall. It follows the existing hole, so it **cannot correct its position**.
Cuts a larger, flat-bottomed step at the mouth of a hole, for a bolt head or a bearing shoulder
Cuts a shallow, flat, round seat on a rough surface, for a nut or washer to sit on
Cuts a cone-shaped recess for a countersunk screw
Cuts a thread inside a hole

blocks.p: The **cutting speed (Vc)** is how fast the cutting edge moves over the metal, in **metres per minute (m/min)**. Each tool material and work material has a cutting speed that suits it, given in the tool maker's chart. The **spindle speed (N)**, in revolutions per minute (rpm), is worked out from it:

blocks.note: **N = (Vc × 1000) ÷ (π × D)**, where N = spindle speed in rpm, Vc = cutting speed in m/min, D = the diameter being cut in mm, and π ≈ 3.142. The 1000 changes metres into millimetres.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Worked example
Working
rows: A 32 mm bore with an HSS tool at 25 m/min
An 80 mm bore with a carbide insert at 120 m/min
≈ **477 rpm**: on a machine with fixed speeds, choose the nearest speed **below**, for example 450 rpm
Facing a 1200 mm flange on a vertical boring mill at 90 m/min

blocks.p: Notice that the **bigger the diameter, the slower the spindle** for the same cutting speed, because the edge of a large circle travels further in each turn.

blocks.note: These are typical figures only. Use the cutting speed from the tool maker's chart and your instructor, and start at the lower end on an old or less rigid machine, a long bar, or a heavy cut.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: On a machine with fixed speeds, choose the nearest speed **below** the worked-out figure, so the tool does not run too fast and burn.
Watch and listen during the first cut. Squealing, chatter, blue chips from steel or a worn edge mean the speed is too high: turn it down.
A dull, rough finish with torn metal and a lump of metal welded on the tool tip (a **built-up edge**) can mean the speed is too low, especially on mild steel and aluminium.

head: Term
Meaning
Typical figures (guide)
rows: How far the tool moves along the bore in each turn of the spindle, in mm per revolution (mm/rev)
Roughing about 0.15–0.3 mm/rev; finishing about 0.05–0.1 mm/rev
How deep the tool cuts into the wall, measured on one side
Roughing as deep as the bar and machine allow without chatter; finishing a light cut of about 0.1–0.25 mm

blocks.p: Bores are cut with **roughing passes** that remove most of the metal quickly, then a **light finishing pass** with a fine feed. A light cut bends the bar less, so the size is more exact and the finish smoother. Rough to about 0.3–0.5 mm under the finished diameter, then finish.

head: Worked example
Working
rows: How long does one pass take along a 40 mm long bore at 250 rpm with a feed of 0.1 mm/rev?

ul: For steel, cutting fluid (usually soluble oil mixed with water as the maker says) **cools** the tool and work, **lubricates** the cut for a better finish, and **flushes chips** out of the bore.
**Cast iron** is usually bored **dry**: its graphite lubricates the cut, and fluid would mix with the dust into a sludge. Use a dust mask and extraction.
Aluminium is usually cut with fluid, which stops metal sticking to the tool.
Carbide tools should not be cooled with a sudden splash of fluid when they are hot: the shock can crack them. Use a steady flow, or none.

blocks.p: A drill is quick, but it follows any hard spot or slope, so drilled holes wander, are slightly out of round and are rarely exactly to size. The boring tool is guided by the machine's spindle, so boring **corrects the hole's position, size, roundness and finish**. A reamer gives a good size and finish, but it follows the existing hole and does not correct its position.

blocks.h: Boring a hole to size in solid metal

flow: Read the drawing; set up, clamp and square the work; find the datum; move to the hole position
Have the set-up checked by the assessor or instructor
Centre drill, so the hole starts in the right place
Drill a pilot hole, then open it up with larger drills, leaving a few millimetres on the diameter for boring
Fit the boring bar or head with the shortest overhang that reaches; set the speed and feed
Take roughing cuts to about 0.3–0.5 mm under size
Stop the spindle, clean the bore, and measure
Adjust the tool by the amount needed; take a light finishing cut with a fine feed
Stop and measure again; take a very light extra cut if needed
Remove the sharp edges, clean the part, and record the sizes

blocks.h: Adjusting a boring head to the final size

blocks.p: The tool cuts on both sides of the hole, so moving the tool out by a certain amount makes the **diameter** grow by **twice** that amount. Move the tool by **half** the change you want in the diameter.

head: Worked example
Working
rows: The drawing gives 32.00 +0.05/−0.00 mm. After roughing, the bore measures 31.82 mm.
Aim for the middle of the tolerance: about 32.02 mm
Move the tool out by 0.20 ÷ 2 = **0.10 mm** on the radius

blocks.note: Some boring heads have dials that read the change in **diameter**, not radius. Read the maker's markings on your head before you adjust it, or you will cut twice as much as you meant to.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: If the bar springs, a second pass at the same setting (a **spring cut**) often removes a little more metal and improves the size and finish. Measure after it.

**Line boring** means boring two or more holes, in different walls of a part, so that they share exactly the **same centre line**. A shaft that runs in bearings in two walls of a gearbox casing, or a pin that passes through both lugs of a bracket, needs holes that are truly in line. If they are not, the shaft bends, bearings run hot and wear out, gears do not mesh properly, and a pin will not go in or wears quickly.

flow: Set the part square on the table and clamp it near the walls to be bored, without distorting them
Line the spindle up with the hole centre
Centre drill and drill through both walls from one set-up, if they need drilling
Pass a long boring bar through both walls; support its far end in the end support
Rough and finish bore every hole **without moving the work**
Stop and measure each hole, then check the alignment with a **test bar** (a ground bar of the right size) that must slide freely through all the holes

blocks.note: Pin bosses on buckets, hinges and brackets are often built up with weld when they wear, then line bored back to size. Weld first, bore after: the welding heat would pull bores made earlier out of line.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Operation
What it does
rows: Machines a flat surface square to the bore, with a facing head or facing slide
Cuts a larger, flat-bottomed step at the mouth of a hole
Cuts a shallow flat seat round a hole on a rough casting, so a nut or washer sits flat
Cuts a small angled edge at the mouth of the bore, to remove the sharp edge and help parts go in
Finishes a hole to an exact size and smooth wall, after drilling or boring
Cuts a thread inside a hole
Machines the outside diameter of round work as it turns on the table

blocks.note: On a vertical boring mill with a fixed table speed, the cutting speed falls as a facing tool moves in towards the centre, because each turn covers a smaller circle. Some machines change the table speed automatically to keep the cutting speed constant.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Stop the spindle (or table) fully.**
Clean the chips and fluid out of the bore.
Let a hot part cool. Steel grows as it warms, by about 0.011 mm on every 100 mm for each 10 °C. A bore measured hot and cut "to size" will be **undersize** when it cools.

head: Instrument
How it is used
Accuracy (typical)
rows: A quick check of a bore. Not accurate enough for close tolerances.
About 0.02 mm, but hard to hold square in a bore
Put the gauge in the bore, let the arms spring out, rock it gently across the bore to find the largest size, lock it, remove it, and measure across it with an outside micrometer.
Reads directly across the bore. Rock it to find the largest reading in one direction.
Set to zero with a setting ring or a micrometer at the size wanted, then rocked in the bore. It shows how far the bore is above or below that size, and shows taper and ovality quickly.
The GO end must enter the bore and the NO GO end must not.
Checks that the bore is within its limits; does not give a size
A ground bar that must slide through in-line holes

ul: At the **top, middle and bottom** of the bore (near each end and in the middle), to find taper or bellmouth.
In **two directions at right angles**, to find ovality.
Write every reading down, and compare it with the drawing.

blocks.p: The **tolerance** is how much a size may vary from the drawing size and still be accepted. The **limits** are the largest and smallest sizes allowed.
Aim for the **middle** of the tolerance on your finishing cut. A bore with all its readings between the limits is accepted. A bore with any reading outside them is not.

ul: A bore that is still **undersize** can be cut again: measure, adjust and take another light cut.
A bore that is **oversize** cannot be put right by cutting. Stop, tag the part, and tell your instructor or supervisor. Never hide it among the good parts, or try to close the bore by hammering it.
Record the sizes on the job sheet, with your name and the date.

head: Fault
What you see
Main causes
Cures
rows: A loud buzz or squeal; a wavy, rough, patterned wall; chipped tool tips
Bar too long or too thin
Blunt tool, or tip shape wrong
Speed too high; cut too light or too heavy
Worn machine slides or spindle bearings
Thickest, shortest bar; support long bars
Clamp tight over solid support; tighten the tool
Lower speed; change feed or depth
The bore is bigger at one end than the other
The bar bending more as it goes deeper
Stiffer, shorter bar; lighter finishing cut; a spring cut
The bore is bigger only at its mouth
The bar springing as the tool enters the cut
Different readings in two directions at right angles
Work clamped too hard and distorted; springs back when released
Clamp over support, no tighter than needed
The bore is bigger than the upper limit
Tool moved out too far (dial misread, or radius and diameter confused)
Not measuring before the finishing cut
Measure, work out the move, check the dial, take light cuts
The bore is smaller than the lower limit
Bar springing away from the cut
Another light cut or spring cut; measure when cool
A rough, torn or scored wall
Sharp tool; fine feed for the last cut
The position does not match the drawing
Approach from one direction; lock slides
Clamp securely; check the work before each hole

ul: Remove the **sharp edges** (burrs) at both ends of the bore with a deburring tool, a scraper or a small chamfer. Sharp edges cut hands and stop shafts, pins and bearings going in.
Clean the part, measure it once more, and record the sizes.
Lift it off with the right lifting gear, label it and put it in the right place.

blocks.h: Caring for the machine at the end of the job

flow: Stop the machine and isolate it as the Centre's rules require
Remove the work with the right lifting gear
Take out the boring bar, head and tools; clean them, check the tips for wear or chips, and store them in their holders. Report or replace worn tips
Clear the chips from the table, T-slots and slides with a brush and chip hook into the chip bin (keep steel and cast-iron chips apart if the Centre recycles them)
Wipe off the cutting fluid; oil the slides and the points the maker's chart shows; check the oil and fluid levels
Put clamps, step blocks and parallels back in their racks; wipe instruments and put them in their cases
Report any fault, such as a strange noise, a leak or a damaged guard, and fill in the machine log
Sweep the floor and wipe up spills so no one slips

blocks.note: Never hose a machine down with water: it rusts the slides and gets into the electrics. Never leave chips and fluid on the table for the next shift.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what boring is and why holes are often bored after drilling or after welding.
I can name the main parts of a horizontal boring machine and a vertical boring mill, say what moves on each, and the work each suits.
I can follow the safety rules for boring machines, including dress, no gloves near turning parts, isolation, chips, fluid and lifting.
I can read a drawing for each hole's size, tolerance, position, finish and datum.
I can lift work safely with rated gear and clamp it on parallels with strap clamps, step blocks and packing set correctly.
I can set work square with a dial indicator, find a datum with an edge finder, and centre on a bore by clocking.
I can choose a rigid boring bar or head and a suitable tool tip.
I can work out a spindle speed from N = (Vc × 1000) ÷ (π × D) and choose the speed to set.
I can set the feed and depth of cut for roughing and finishing, and use cutting fluid correctly.
I can drill and bore a hole to size, adjusting a boring head by half the diameter change.
I can explain line boring and check in-line holes with a test bar.
I can measure a bore with a telescopic gauge and micrometer, an inside micrometer or a bore gauge, at several depths and in two directions.
I can say whether a size is within its tolerance, and what to do when it is not.
I can recognise chatter, taper, bellmouth, ovality and poor finish, and say how to cure them.
I can deburr the part, clean and lubricate the machine, store the tools and report faults.

terms: Backlash
Play in a handwheel screw, which can put a slide out of position
Bellmouth
A bore that is larger at its mouth than further in
Boring
Enlarging a hole with a single-point tool to an exact size, position and finish
Boring bar
A bar holding a cutting tool that cuts the inside of a hole
Boring head
An adjustable holder in the spindle that moves the tool out in small, exact steps
Built-up edge
Metal welded onto the tool tip, which spoils the finish
Centre drill
A short, stiff drill used to start a hole in the right place
Chatter
Vibration of the tool against the work, leaving a wavy, rough surface
Counterbore
A larger, flat-bottomed step at the mouth of a hole
Cutting speed (Vc)
How fast the cutting edge moves over the metal, in m/min
Datum
The face, edge or point that positions are measured from
Edge finder
A tool held in the spindle to find the edge of the work and set a datum
End support
The column that supports the outer end of a long boring bar
Eyebolt
A lifting fitting with a ring, screwed into a tapped hole in the work
Feed
How far the tool moves along per turn of the spindle, in mm/rev
Headstock
The part of a horizontal boring machine that carries the spindle up and down the column
Insert
A small carbide tip clamped in a holder and turned to a fresh edge when worn
Line boring
Boring holes in separate walls on one centre line in one set-up
Ovality
A bore that is slightly oval, not round; also called out of round
Parallels
A matched pair of accurate bars used to raise the work evenly off the table
Reamer
A fluted tool that finishes a hole to an exact size and smooth wall
Safe working load (SWL)
The largest load a sling, eyebolt or crane may lift
Spot facing
Cutting a flat seat round a hole on a rough surface
Spring cut
A repeat pass at the same setting to remove metal left by the bar springing
Step block
A stepped block that supports the end of a clamp at the right height
Strap clamp
A flat bar clamp with a bolt in the middle and packing at one end
T-slot
A slotted groove in a machine table that holds clamping bolts
Taper
A bore that is larger at one end than the other
Telescopic gauge
A sprung gauge locked across a bore, then measured with a micrometer
Tolerance
How much a size may vary from the drawing size and still be accepted
Vertical boring mill
A machine like a lathe on end, where the work turns on a large table; also called a vertical turret lathe (VTL)

c1.title: A pump casing on the horizontal borer in Kingston
c1.text: Rushane is an apprentice at an engineering shop in Kingston. He must bore the 80 mm bearing seat of a grey cast-iron pump casing that weighs about 180 kg, on the horizontal boring machine. The drawing gives 80.00 +0.03/−0.00 mm. The tool maker's chart gives 100 m/min for his carbide insert in cast iron, and the machine's speeds are 280, 355, 450 and 560 rpm. He has clamped the casing with strap clamps, but one packing block is about 20 mm lower than the casing's clamping face.

c2.title: A large flange on the vertical mill in Clarendon
c2.text: Kerry-Ann is a trainee in a sugar factory's machine shop in Clarendon. She is facing and boring a steel flange 1200 mm across, held in the jaws of the vertical boring mill's table. Two of the jaws stick out past the edge of the table. The flange has a heavy lifting lug welded on one side. Her carbide tool is to run at about 90 m/min.

c3.title: Re-boring a bucket's pin bosses in Yallahs
c3.text: Oneil works at a plant-hire workshop in Yallahs, St Thomas. The pin bosses of a backhoe bucket have worn oval, and the welder has built them up with weld. The two bosses are 600 mm apart, and both must now be bored to 60.00 +0.05/−0.00 mm so that one pin passes through both. Oneil sets the bucket up on the horizontal boring machine with a long boring bar. After roughing, the first boss measures 59.84 mm. His boring head's dial reads the tool's movement on the radius.

c4.title: Checking a bore at the training centre in Bog Walk
c4.text: Tamara is a trainee at a training centre in Bog Walk, St Catherine. She has bored a hole in a mild steel block to a drawing size of 45.00 +0.04/−0.00 mm. Straight after her finishing cut, with the block still warm, she measures with a telescopic gauge and micrometer: 45.07 mm at the top, 45.02 mm in the middle and 45.02 mm at the bottom.

questions.q: Which spindle speed should Rushane set for the 80 mm bore?
o: 280 rpm
355 rpm
450 rpm
560 rpm
questions.why: N = (100 × 1000) ÷ (3.142 × 80) ≈ 398 rpm. The machine cannot give 398, so he takes the nearest speed below, 355 rpm, rather than run the tool too fast at 450.

questions.q: What is likely to happen with the packing block 20 mm lower than the casing's clamping face?
o: The clamp presses down harder and holds the casing better
Nothing, provided the T-bolt is tightened fully
The clamp tilts and holds only on its edge
The casing is lifted off the table at that corner
questions.why: The packing should be level with or just above the clamping face so the clamp presses down squarely. A low packing block tips the clamp, so it holds on a small edge and can let the work shift under the cut.

questions.q: Why should Rushane put each clamp's T-bolt close to the casing rather than close to the packing?
o: So more of the clamping force goes onto the casing
So the clamp is easier to undo at the end of the job
So the T-bolt does not touch the hot cutting fluid
So the boring bar can pass over the top of the clamp
questions.why: The clamp acts like a lever, sharing the bolt's force between the work and the packing. The nearer the bolt is to the work, the bigger the share that holds the work down.

questions.q: Running a dial indicator along the casing's machined datum face reads 0.00 mm at one end and 0.12 mm at the other. What should Rushane do?
o: Bore it as it is, since 0.12 mm is too small to matter
Tap it round until the reading is even, then reclamp
Reset the dial to zero at the far end and start boring
Add a thicker parallel under the low end of the casing
questions.why: The changing reading shows the face is not square to the spindle, so the bore would not be true to the part. He taps the casing round until the reading stays the same, tightens the clamps, and checks again.

questions.q: About what table speed suits Kerry-Ann's 90 m/min at the outside edge of the 1200 mm flange?
o: About 2.4 rpm
About 75 rpm
About 240 rpm
About 24 rpm
questions.why: N = (90 × 1000) ÷ (3.142 × 1200) = 90 000 ÷ 3770 ≈ 24 rpm. Large work turns slowly, because its edge travels a long way in each turn.

questions.q: Two jaws stick out past the edge of the table. What must be in place before the table turns?
o: A barrier or guard rail that keeps people clear of the jaws
Chalk marks on the jaws so the operator can see them turning
A slower feed on the rail head so the jaws turn more slowly
Rags tied over the jaws so they cannot catch on clothing
questions.why: Turning jaws that stick out beyond the table can strike or drag in anyone near them. A barrier keeps people out of their reach; rags or marks do nothing to stop an injury.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann faces the flange from its outside edge in towards the centre, with the table speed fixed. What happens to the cutting speed?
o: It rises as the tool moves inwards
It stays the same across the face
It falls as the tool moves inwards
It rises at first, then stays the same
questions.why: At a fixed table speed, a point near the centre travels round a smaller circle in each turn, so the edge meets the metal more slowly. Some machines speed the table up as the tool moves in to keep the cutting speed constant.

questions.q: The flange has a heavy lug on one side. What must Kerry-Ann check before running the table at speed?
o: That the lug is painted so it shows up when turning
That the work is balanced and every jaw is tight
That cutting fluid is flowing onto the lug
That the rail head is set at its highest position
questions.why: A heavy lug on one side makes the turning work out of balance, which shakes the machine and can loosen the jaws. Check every jaw is tight, and balance the work or keep the speed low as the instructor directs.

questions.q: Why are the bosses bored after the weld build-up, and not before?
o: Weld metal is too hard to bore once it has cooled
Boring first would leave no room for the weld metal
The welder needs a rough hole to strike the arc in
Welding heat would pull earlier bores out of line
questions.why: Weld metal shrinks as it cools and pulls the part out of shape. Boring after welding means the finished holes are in line, at the right size, whatever the welding did.

questions.q: The bosses are 600 mm apart, and the long bar sags and chatters at its far end. What should Oneil do?
o: Run the spindle faster so the bar stiffens up
Support the far end of the bar in the end support
Bore each boss from its own side with a short bar
Take heavier cuts so the bar is pushed against the work
questions.why: A long bar held at one end bends under the cut. Supporting its far end in the end support makes it stiff, and keeps both bores on the same centre line from one set-up.

questions.q: The first boss measures 59.84 mm after roughing. How far should Oneil move the tool out to finish at about 60.02 mm?
questions.why: The diameter must grow by 60.02 − 59.84 = 0.18 mm. The tool cuts on both sides, so on a radius dial it moves out half of that: 0.09 mm.

questions.q: Both bosses measure within the tolerance. How should Oneil check that they are in line?
o: Measure each bore again in two directions
Look through both bores against a light
Slide a test bar through both bosses
Measure from each bore to the bucket's edge
questions.why: Two bores can each be the right size and still be out of line. A ground test bar (or the pin) that slides freely through both proves they share one centre line.

questions.q: Which of Tamara's readings is outside the drawing's limits?
o: The top, at 45.07 mm
The middle, at 45.02 mm
The bottom, at 45.02 mm
None of them is outside
questions.why: The limits are 45.00 mm and 45.04 mm. The middle and bottom readings are within them; 45.07 mm at the top is over the upper limit.

questions.q: What is the name of the fault her readings show?
o: Taper
Ovality
Chatter marks
Bellmouth
questions.why: The bore is the same size in the middle and at the bottom, and larger only at its mouth: a bellmouth. It usually comes from the bar springing as the tool enters the cut.

questions.q: Tamara measured while the block was still warm. What will the bore do as the block cools?
o: It will get larger
It will not change
It will go slightly oval
It will get smaller
questions.why: Steel expands when warm and shrinks as it cools, and a hole in it shrinks too. Measure when the part has cooled, or a bore cut "to size" warm will be undersize later.

questions.q: How should Tamara use the telescopic gauge to find the true diameter?
o: Push it in square, lock it at once, and read the scale on its handle
Rock it across the bore to find the largest size, then lock
Lock it, then tap it into the bore until it is tight
Hold it at a slant across the bore so both arms touch the wall
questions.why: The true diameter is the largest distance across the bore. Rocking the gauge lets the arms settle at that size before it is locked, removed and measured with an outside micrometer.

questions.q: As a guide, about how far may a 25 mm solid steel boring bar stick out from its holder?
o: About 25 mm
About 50 mm
About 100 mm
About 250 mm
questions.why: A common guide is no more than about four times the bar's diameter for a solid steel bar: 4 × 25 = 100 mm. Further out, it bends and chatters; carbide and damped bars can reach further, as their makers say.

questions.q: A bolt hole in a rough cast surface needs a flat seat for a nut and washer. Which operation gives it?
o: Countersinking
Reaming
Spot facing
Tapping
questions.why: Spot facing cuts a shallow, flat, round seat on a rough surface so a nut or washer sits square. A countersink makes a cone for a countersunk screw, and a reamer only sizes the hole.

questions.q: A drilled hole is 1 mm out of position. Why can a reamer not put it right?
o: A reamer cuts too slowly to remove 1 mm
A reamer can only be used in cast-iron parts
A reamer only works on holes over 50 mm
It follows the hole that is already there
questions.why: A reamer sizes and smooths the existing hole, following wherever it goes. Only a boring tool, guided by the spindle, can move the hole's centre to the right place.

questions.q: Leon is lifting a casting with an eyebolt. Which check matters most before the lift?
o: It is screwed fully in, with its collar seated
It has been painted a bright colour so it shows
It is the longest eyebolt in the rack
It is loose enough to swivel round freely
questions.why: An eyebolt holds its rated load only when it is screwed fully into a sound thread with its collar seated and the pull in line. A part-screwed or side-loaded eyebolt can bend or tear out.
